backend.title: What is a backend?
backend.intro: At 8:03 on the bus, you add The Hobbit to your book club’s reading list. At 8:04, Mira opens the list on her laptop and there it is. Your phone has never met her laptop. They have, however, been talking to the same backend.

steps.title: Two screens, one bookshelf
steps.body:
Picture the list on your phone. Everything you can point at belongs to the interface: the title field, the little cover image, the Save button that moves just enough to reassure your thumb. The frontend is the code that draws those things and reacts when you use them. It can show The Hobbit immediately because it already knows what you typed.

Now put the phone in airplane mode before tapping Save. The interface can still draw a perfectly convincing book. How would Mira’s laptop learn about it? A change on one device needs a way to reach a place both devices can consult. For this app, that place is a service running on a computer reachable over the network. The program doing that shared work is the backend.

steps.title: What travels when you tap Save?
steps.body:
The phone sends a request. Think of it as a short note with an address and a job. The address names the club’s list; the job is to add a book. The message carries the title and enough information for the service to recognize your signed-in session. The cover animation stays on the phone. Nobody needs to post a tiny picture of your thumb to the server.

Here is a simplified version of that note. POST is the action, the path identifies the collection of books, and the text between braces is the data. Read it aloud as “please add this title to the Tuesday club’s books.”
steps.code:
POST /clubs/tuesday/books

{"title": "The Hobbit"}

steps.title: The server has a decision to make
steps.body:
A server is something that listens for requests and answers them. One physical computer can run several server programs. In this story, the bookshelf program receives the note and picks the piece of code responsible for adding books. That piece of code is called a handler.

Suppose yesterday you could edit the list, but this morning the club made you a guest. Your phone might still have yesterday’s screen open, complete with its optimistic little Save button. The handler looks up your current membership and checks whether it allows edits. It also checks the title. A signed-in editor who submits six spaces has still failed to recommend a book. These decisions are examples of backend logic.

steps.title: Where the book spends the night
steps.body:
Once the request passes those checks, the handler asks a database to store an entry containing the club, the book title, and a new identifier. An identifier matters because two books can share a title, and next week someone might correct a spelling mistake. The entry needs an identity that survives the edit.

Why involve a database? The running program could keep a list in memory, which is handy for a quick experiment. Restart that program and its in-memory list disappears. A database can keep committed records on durable storage. After a restart the service can read the list again. The backend makes the decision to save; the database does the remembering.

steps.title: What Mira actually sees
steps.body:
After the database confirms the write, the handler replies to your phone. In this example, 201 means the service created a new entry. The phone can now replace “Saving…” with “Saved.”

Mira opening the list produces a second, independent request. Her browser asks for Tuesday’s books. The service checks that she may read the list, fetches its entries, and returns data. Her frontend turns that data into the row she sees. If Mira already had the page open, she might have to refresh it: sharing a database gives both devices a common record, while live screen updates require the app to fetch or receive changes.
steps.code:
201 Created
{"id": 42, "title": "The Hobbit"}

steps.title: A small mystery to solve
steps.body:
Your phone displays The Hobbit. You close the app, reopen it, and the book is gone. Mira never saw it either. Which fact would you check first?

Find out whether the server confirmed the save. The phone might have drawn the row while offline, the server might have declined the edit, or the write might have failed. Seeing a row tells you what the interface displayed. Seeing the server’s response gives you evidence about how far the change travelled.

steps.title: In short
steps.body: The frontend takes your tap. The backend checks what it means and whether it’s allowed. The database remembers the result so another device can ask for it later.

lifecycle.title: The request lifecycle
lifecycle.intro: Mira opens book 42. One title appears on her screen. Follow that single lookup and watch how the question changes hands.

steps.title: The browser asks a question
steps.body:
Mira taps a book in the list. Her browser knows its identifier, 42, but needs its details. It sends an HTTP request. HTTP gives the browser and server a shared way to describe an action and send back the outcome. Here GET means read, and the path says which book to read.

Imagine ordering “the usual” in a café you’ve never visited. The staff needs something more specific. The path serves that purpose: the same server might also answer requests for clubs, members, and reading lists.
steps.code: GET /books/42

steps.title: The route finds the right handler
steps.body:
The server matches the method and path to a route for reading one book. The route has a slot for an identifier. For this request, the slot holds 42. The handler receives that value and applies the rules for this lookup. On a private bookshelf, one rule is that Mira must be allowed to see the book.

At this point the server knows what Mira wants. It still needs to find out whether book 42 exists.
steps.code:
GET /books/:id
This request supplies id = 42

steps.title: The handler looks up the record
steps.body:
The handler asks storage for the record whose identifier is 42. In a relational database, the query below selects just the title. The placeholder carries the identifier as a separate value. A document database can answer the same question using its own query language.

If storage returns a record, the handler can build an answer. An empty result is useful information too. A working database can quite accurately report that it has never heard of book 42.
steps.code:
SELECT title FROM books WHERE id = $1
Parameter: 42

steps.title: The response goes home
steps.body:
The handler returns a status and a body. The status tells the browser how the request went. The body carries the book data. Mira’s browser reads the title and draws it in the details panel. The request is now complete. Opening another book starts another trip.

Try predicting two other endings. If the book has been deleted, the service might return 404 so the browser can say “Book not found.” If storage is temporarily unavailable, the service should report a failure instead. Telling Mira her book vanished because a database is having a bad afternoon would make for a very strange book club.
steps.code:
200 OK
{"title": "The Hobbit"}

steps.title: In short
steps.body: Browser asks. Handler checks. Storage answers. Server replies. The browser turns that reply into something Mira can read.

runtime.title: Run your first Node.js program
runtime.intro: Node.js runs JavaScript outside a browser. Start with a file that prints one line, before opening a network connection.

steps.title: Check the runtime
steps.body: Install Node.js from nodejs.org, open a terminal, and check that your shell can find it. A version number means you can run a script.
steps.code: node --version

steps.title: Run a file
steps.body: Save the first line below in hello.mjs. Run the command from the same folder. Edit the message and run it again to see where the output comes from.

steps.title: Inspect the process
steps.body: Type node in your terminal to open its interactive prompt. Evaluate the expression below to see the folder your program starts in. Type .exit to leave.
steps.code: process.cwd()

modules.title: Organize code and packages
modules.intro: Split book formatting from the script that uses it.

steps.title: Export a function
steps.body: Save this in book.mjs. A named export makes the function available to other modules.

steps.title: Import it
steps.body: Save this in main.mjs beside book.mjs and run node main.mjs. The relative path identifies your local module.
steps.code:
import { label } from './book.mjs';
console.log(label({ title: 'Dune' }));

steps.title: Manage dependencies
steps.body: Run npm init -y in a new project folder to create package.json. npm install followed by a package name records that dependency. Commit the lockfile so teammates can reproduce the resolved versions.
steps.code:
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev typescript

async.title: Files, promises, and the event loop
async.intro: Predict the three messages before you run this example in an .mjs file.

steps.title: Start a read
steps.body: A file read takes time. The promise represents its eventual result. Node can continue running the rest of this script while the read is pending.

steps.title: Yield and resume
steps.body: Append these lines. The first two messages are start and pending. After the read completes, the suspended function resumes and reports the character count.

steps.title: Handle failure
steps.body: Try reading a missing file inside a try block. A rejected promise at an await jumps to catch. Long synchronous calculations still occupy the JavaScript thread and delay other handlers.
steps.code:
try { await readFile('missing.txt'); }
catch (error) { console.error(error.message); }

http.title: Serve an HTTP response
http.intro: Turn a script that exits into a process that listens for requests.

steps.title: Start listening
steps.body: Save this as server.mjs and run node server.mjs. listen keeps the process waiting for connections on your computer.

steps.title: Inspect the exchange
steps.body: Open this address in a browser. Refresh it and the handler runs again. In the browser Network panel inspect the status, content type, and body. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.

streams.title: Streams and events
streams.intro: A large file can travel through a program one chunk at a time.

steps.title: Connect a pipeline
steps.body: Put books.txt beside this .mjs script, then run the script in that folder. The pipeline reads chunks and writes a copy. Await its promise to detect completion or catch failures.

steps.title: Match the reader to the writer
steps.body: A slow destination needs time to drain its buffer. The pipeline regulates the reader so it can process a file larger than the available memory.
steps.code: source → buffered chunks → destination

steps.title: Listen for an event
steps.body: An event emitter lets a producer notify listeners. Register the listener first. Each emit below calls it with the supplied title.

operate.title: Configure, debug, and test
operate.intro: Make the reading-list service easier to run and check.

steps.title: Read configuration
steps.body: Environment variables arrive as strings. This expression chooses a port when PORT is missing and converts it to a number. Validate the range before passing user-supplied configuration to listen.
steps.code: const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);

steps.title: Inspect a running script
steps.body: Launch the server with the inspector and a breakpoint at startup. Attach a Node debugger, step into the handler, and inspect req.url when a request arrives.
steps.code: node --inspect-brk server.mjs

steps.title: Test a rule
steps.body: Put this in book.test.mjs beside book.mjs from the modules lesson. Run node --test. Change the expected value and read the difference in the failure report.

js-books.title: Write a book handler in JavaScript
js-books.intro: Give your API one rule: a book must have a nonempty title.

steps.title: Define the boundary
steps.body: Incoming JSON can contain any value. Check its shape before calling string methods.

steps.title: Try two inputs
steps.body: Save the function and these calls in book.mjs. Run node book.mjs. The first call prints Dune and the second reports the validation error.
steps.code:
console.log(titleOf(' Dune '));
try { titleOf(42); } catch { console.log('Invalid title'); }

documents.title: Store books in MongoDB
documents.intro: Use mongosh connected to a local MongoDB instance.

steps.title: Model a book
steps.body: Switch to a practice database. Each book will be a document in the books collection. MongoDB creates the collection on its first insert.
steps.code: use reading_list

steps.title: Save and read
steps.body: Insert a document and find it by title. Keep the generated identifier to update this exact book.
steps.code:
const book = db.books.insertOne({title: 'Dune', finished: false});
db.books.findOne({_id: book.insertedId})

steps.title: Update and delete
steps.body: Mark this book as finished. Read it back before removing the practice document.
steps.code:
db.books.updateOne({_id: book.insertedId}, {$set: {finished: true}})
db.books.findOne({_id: book.insertedId})
db.books.deleteOne({_id: book.insertedId})

typed-books.title: Write a book handler in TypeScript
typed-books.intro: Give your API one rule: a book must have a nonempty title.

steps.title: Define the boundary
steps.body: Incoming JSON can contain any value. Check its shape before calling string methods.

steps.title: Try two inputs
steps.body: Save the function and these calls in book.ts. Install TypeScript with npm install -D typescript, then run npx tsc --strict book.ts and node book.js. Observe which checks still happen at runtime.
steps.code:
console.log(titleOf(' Dune '));
try { titleOf(42); } catch { console.log('Invalid title'); }

tables.title: Store books in PostgreSQL
tables.intro: Use psql connected to a practice PostgreSQL database.

steps.title: Model a book
steps.body: Create a table. Each row needs an identifier and a title. A primary key lets the database distinguish two books with the same title.
steps.code: CREATE TABLE books (id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, title text NOT NULL, finished boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false);

steps.title: Save and read
steps.body: Insert a row and read the generated id. Use it in the next step to select the intended row.
steps.code:
INSERT INTO books (title) VALUES ('Dune') RETURNING id;
SELECT id, title FROM books WHERE title = 'Dune';

steps.title: Update and delete
steps.body: Replace 1 with the returned id. Mark the book finished, inspect the row, then remove the practice record.
steps.code:
UPDATE books SET finished = true WHERE id = 1 RETURNING *;
DELETE FROM books WHERE id = 1;
